digest.top_line: RTOG 3506 (STEEL): enzalutamide added to SRT + 24mo GnRHa for high-risk BCR post-RP → PFS HR 0.62 (80% CI 0.42-0.91), randomized phase II screening signal.
digest.tldr: Prostate was the only site today, and both trials change the hormonal partner given with RT. STEEL points to enza intensification of salvage RT + 24mo GnRHa, but only at a phase II screening threshold (one-sided p=0.052 vs α 0.10), and SRT parameters are unreported. REVELUTION favors relugolix over leuprolide on 12-mo IPSS and EPIC-CP total, in a post hoc analysis with N=65.

sites.intro: Both studies modify the ADT backbone paired with RT, not the RT itself; RT dose, fractionation and nodal coverage go unreported in both sources.

studies.name: REVELUTION
studies.tldr: Relugolix vs leuprolide with RT: 12-mo IPSS 5.66 vs 9.22 (p=0.039) and EPIC-CP total 12.25 vs 17.25 (p=0.02), post hoc PRO analysis.
details: 🔍 Randomized 1:1, N=65, relugolix (oral daily) vs leuprolide (q3mo injection), each with RT
🔍 Localized intermediate- or high-risk prostate cancer, no prior ADT
⚠️ Parent trial 1° EP was 12-mo change in total coronary plaque volume by coronary CTA; this QoL analysis is post hoc
📊 Mean testosterone at 12 mo: 199.7 vs 142.0 ng/dL relugolix vs leuprolide, p=0.01

details.text: 📊 12-mo PROs, relugolix vs leuprolide (covariate-adjusted means, lower = better)

details: 📊 EPIC-CP bowel and vitality domains also plotted (P=.003 and P=.053); per-domain values not cleanly attributable from source OCR
📊 No significant 12-mo difference in EPIC-CP incontinence, irritation, sexual, or SHIM (P .15 to .92)
⚠️ Small N, unblinded route of administration (oral vs injection) with self-reported endpoints
⚠️ ADT duration not clearly legible in source; higher 12-mo testosterone likely reflects faster recovery, not confirmed in source text

figures.caption: IPSS at 12 months: 5.7 vs 9.2. EPIC-CP total at 12 months: 12.3 vs 17.3 (P = .020).
Mean testosterone at 12 months: 199.7 relugolix vs 142.0 leuprolide, P= .010.
Schema: 65 randomized 1:1, leuprolide + RT vs relugolix + RT.

verdict.rationale: Post hoc QoL analysis of a trial powered for coronary plaque volume; N=65, open-label route difference with patient-reported endpoints.
verdict.audience: Localized intermediate/high-risk prostate, ADT-naive, receiving RT + ADT

studies.significance: The PRO gap tracks testosterone: relugolix pts sat at 199.7 vs 142.0 ng/dL at 12 mo, and urinary (IPSS) plus EPIC-CP total scores favored relugolix, while sexual and continence domains did not separate. For a short-course ADT + RT plan, this informs agent choice on recovery and urinary symptom burden, not oncologic control.
studies.monday_clinic: In ADT-naive localized intermediate- or high-risk prostate cancer starting RT with ADT, this supports weighing relugolix over leuprolide for 12-mo urinary symptom burden and testosterone recovery; it does not inform cancer control or sexual function outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Randomized 1:1, **N=65**, relugolix vs leuprolide with RT. Parent trial **primary endpoint: 12-month change in total coronary plaque volume** by coronary CTA; this PRO analysis is **post hoc**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Localized intermediate- or high-risk prostate cancer**, **no prior ADT**, planned for RT + ADT.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Relugolix oral daily vs leuprolide injection every 3 months, each combined with RT.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: IPSS, EPIC-CP domains (total, bowel, vitality, incontinence, irritation, sexual) and SHIM, reported as covariate-adjusted means to 12 months; mean testosterone.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: At 12 mo relugolix favored on testosterone (**199.7 vs 142.0 ng/dL, p=0.01**), **IPSS 5.66 vs 9.22 (p=0.039)** and **EPIC-CP total 12.25 vs 17.25 (p=0.02)**. Incontinence, irritation, sexual and SHIM showed **no significant difference**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: HERO established relugolix vs leuprolide in advanced disease; this adds a PRO read in the localized RT setting, where ADT is time-limited and recovery matters more.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ADT-naive localized intermediate- or high-risk prostate cancer receiving RT with time-limited ADT. Does not represent metastatic or castration-resistant disease, or oncologic endpoints.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Self-reported outcomes with an unmasked oral vs injectable difference invite expectation bias. Multiple PRO domains tested without stated multiplicity control; the vitality signal is borderline (P=.053).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The plausible mechanism is faster testosterone recovery after a GnRH antagonist, consistent with the 12-mo testosterone gap. Whether it holds with longer ADT courses, or translates into durable QoL beyond 12 mo, is unsettled.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest reading of REVELUTION is pharmacologic rather than oncologic. Relugolix is an oral GnRH antagonist with a short half-life, and the expectation from its development program, including HERO in advanced disease, is that testosterone comes back sooner once it is stopped. Here, at 12 months after ADT initiation, mean testosterone was 199.7 ng/dL with relugolix vs 142.0 with leuprolide (p=0.01), and the patient-reported measures that moved in the same window were urinary symptom burden (IPSS 5.66 vs 9.22) and the EPIC-CP total (12.25 vs 17.25). That coherence between a biochemical difference and a symptom difference is the strongest argument that the PRO signal is real rather than noise.

The weaknesses are structural. The parent trial was designed around coronary plaque volume by CT angiography, so the QoL comparison is post hoc and its N of 65 was never chosen to detect a PRO difference. Several domains were examined, and only some separated, with vitality borderline (P=.053) and the sexual, continence, irritation and SHIM domains null. Without stated multiplicity handling, a reader should treat the two positive composites as hypothesis-generating. The route of administration is also visible to the patient: daily oral therapy vs a quarterly injection is not blinded, and self-reported endpoints are the most exposed to expectation effects.

It is also worth asking why sexual function did not track testosterone. A plausible explanation is that sexual recovery after RT plus ADT is slower and more multifactorial than urinary symptom recovery, and 12 months may be too early, or 65 pts too few, to see it. The null sexual domains should not be read as evidence of no difference.

For the radiation oncologist choosing an ADT agent to pair with RT in localized intermediate- or high-risk disease, the decision this informs is narrow: agent selection on tolerability and recovery, not on cancer control, which this analysis does not address. Adherence to a daily oral drug, cardiovascular considerations that motivated the parent trial, and access all sit alongside it. The result would be wrong, or at least overstated, if the PRO gaps reflect unblinded expectation or chance across multiple domains; a prespecified PRO endpoint in a larger cohort, with ADT duration stratified, is what would settle it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The PRO gap tracks testosterone: relugolix pts sat at 199.7 vs 142.0 ng/dL at 12 mo, and IPSS plus EPIC-CP total favored relugolix while sexual and continence domains did not separate. For ADT + RT in localized disease, this informs agent choice on recovery and urinary burden, not oncologic control.

open_questions: Does the PRO benefit hold with longer ADT courses?
Durability of QoL differences beyond 12 months
Does faster testosterone recovery affect oncologic outcomes with RT?

This study is testing the way that approved androgen deprivation therapy treatments, Leuprolide and Relugolix, for prostate cancer affect quality of life, blood levels, cholesterol, and blood sugar. The drugs are already standard treatment for people with prostate cancer, and the drugs will be used as described in their label.

The names of the study drugs involved in this study are:

* Leuprolide (type of ADT)
* Relugolix (type of ADT)

studies.name: RTOG 3506 (STEEL)
studies.tldr: PFS HR 0.62 (80% CI 0.42-0.91, one-sided p=0.052) adding 24mo enzalutamide to SRT + 24mo GnRHa in high-risk BCR post-RP.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase II, 1:1, n=188, mFU 33.1 mos

details.text: 🔍 Eligibility: BCR after RP plus ≥1 aggressive feature
subdetails: PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL (or ≥0.1 ng/mL on ultrasensitive assay)
Persistently elevated PSA post-RP >0.1 ng/mL, or PSA ≥0.7 ng/mL

details: 📐 Designed with one-sided type I error 0.10, so p=0.052 clears the prespecified bar
📊 Biochemical failure at 2 yrs: 11% vs 19% (enza + ADT vs ADT)
⚠️ 80% CI and one-sided α 0.10 are screening-design thresholds, not phase III evidence
⚠️ SRT dose, fractionation and pelvic nodal coverage not reported in source
⚠️ No metastasis, HRD or survival results reported in source; secondary EPs pending
🔗 Control arm already intensified (24mo GnRHa), longer than the ADT durations tested in RTOG 9601 or GETUG-AFU 16

figures.caption: Progression free survival: HR 0.62, 80% CI 0.42-0.91, one-sided p=0.052.
Primary endpoint: PFS (one-sided type I error=0.10). SRT + 24 months GnRHa ± enzalutamide 160 mg.

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase II screening design (one-sided α 0.10, 80% CI), n=188; positive PFS signal warrants phase III before ARSI intensification with SRT becomes standard.
verdict.audience: High-risk BCR after RP (Gleason 8-10, SVI, pN1 or PSA ≥0.7), receiving SRT

studies.significance: Biochemical failure at 2 yrs fell from 19% to 11% even against a control already carrying 24mo GnRHa, so enzalutamide adds on top of long-course ADT rather than replacing it. SRT dose and nodal volume were not reported, which leaves open whether the gain holds with modern pelvic nodal SRT.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-RP BCR with Gleason 8-10, SVI, pN1 or PSA ≥0.7 heading to SRT with 24mo ADT, this supports discussing ARSI intensification as hypothesis-level evidence; it does not address lower-risk BCR or shorter ADT courses.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized phase II**, 1:1, **n=188**, median follow-up **33.1 mos**. Designed with **one-sided type I error 0.10**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **BCR after RP** with PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL (≥0.1 ng/mL ultrasensitive) plus **≥1 aggressive feature**: Gleason 8-10, SVI, pN1, persistently elevated post-RP PSA >0.1 ng/mL, or PSA ≥0.7 ng/mL.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: SRT + **24 months GnRHa** vs SRT + 24 months GnRHa + **enzalutamide 160 mg** for 24 months.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SRT in both arms. **Dose, fractionation and target volume (prostate bed vs pelvic nodes) not reported in source.**

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** PFS. **Secondary:** biochemical failure, hormone-refractory disease, distant metastasis, cause-specific and overall mortality, physician- and patient-reported toxicity, fatigue (PROMIS-F SF 7a), QoL (EQ-5D-5L).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **PFS HR 0.62**, 80% CI 0.42-0.91, one-sided p=0.052. **Biochemical failure at 2 yrs 11% vs 19%**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: All-grade hot flashes 81% vs 70%, lymphocyte count decreased 21% vs 11%, WBC decreased 17% vs 8%. Fatigue similar at **70% vs 67%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 9601 and GETUG-AFU 16 established hormonal therapy with SRT; SPPORT tested pelvic nodal RT with short-term ADT. STEEL asks the next question, ARSI on top of an already **long-course** ADT backbone.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents high-risk post-RP BCR (Gleason 8-10, SVI, pN1 or PSA ≥0.7) receiving SRT with 24mo GnRHa. Does not represent low-risk BCR, short-course ADT, or PSMA-PET-selected cohorts with a stated imaging gate.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Metastasis, HRD and survival endpoints not reported in source. RT technique unknown, so interaction with pelvic nodal coverage cannot be judged.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A positive screening phase II on a surrogate: it justifies a phase III of ARSI with SRT, but whether PFS gains translate to metastasis or survival is unsettled.

studies.interpretation:
STEEL sits at the point where salvage prostate RT has been accumulating systemic intensification for two decades. RTOG 9601 and GETUG-AFU 16 made hormonal therapy a reasonable partner to SRT, and SPPORT pushed the radiation field outward to the pelvic nodes with short-course ADT. What none of those trials asked is whether a modern androgen receptor pathway inhibitor adds anything once the ADT backbone is already long. STEEL's control arm is not a weak comparator: 24 months of GnRHa with SRT is itself an aggressive regimen for post-prostatectomy recurrence. Seeing a PFS HR of 0.62 and a 2-year biochemical failure rate of 11% versus 19% against that backbone is the most interesting feature of the result, because it argues the benefit is not simply a duration-of-castration effect.

The statistical frame needs to be read for what it is. The trial was built as a randomized screening phase II with one-sided type I error of 0.10, and the result is reported with an 80% confidence interval of 0.42 to 0.91 and a one-sided p of 0.052. That clears the prespecified threshold, and it is an honest positive within its design, but the design exists to decide whether a phase III is worth running, not to change practice. A 95% interval on the same data would be wider and would likely cross 1. With 188 men, a handful of events moving between arms could shift the estimate meaningfully. The tweet and slide also disagree on the lower CI bound (0.41 vs 0.42), a minor point that nonetheless reminds the reader this is a conference presentation, not a peer-reviewed report.

The endpoint is the second constraint. PFS in a BCR population is dominated by PSA events, and the biochemical failure difference is the most concrete number presented. Enzalutamide suppressing PSA during and shortly after a 24-month course is close to expected pharmacology. The question that matters for practice is whether that suppression delays metastasis and hormone-refractory disease after drug cessation. Those endpoints are listed among the secondaries, but no results for them appear in the source, and at a median follow-up of 33.1 months, most men have only recently come off therapy.

For a radiation oncologist, the missing piece is the radiation itself. The source gives no SRT dose, fractionation, or statement on pelvic nodal coverage. That matters because the eligible population (Gleason 8-10, SVI, pN1, or PSA ≥0.7) is exactly the group in whom nodal coverage is most often added, and an ARSI benefit could look different depending on how much occult nodal disease the field already treats. It also leaves open how PSMA PET staging, increasingly standard before SRT, would have reshaped eligibility.

Toxicity looks tolerable on the all-grade table: fatigue was essentially unchanged and hot flashes rose modestly, with more lymphopenia and leukopenia in the enzalutamide arm. The practical read is that STEEL makes ARSI plus SRT plus long-course ADT a credible candidate for a definitive trial in high-risk post-RP recurrence. It does not yet support adding enzalutamide routinely, and it says nothing about lower-risk BCR or shorter ADT courses.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Enzalutamide lowered 2-yr biochemical failure from 19% to 11% on top of SRT with 24mo GnRHa. SRT dose and nodal volume were not reported, so whether the gain persists with pelvic nodal SRT in pN1 or SVI pts is untested.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Benefit came against a 24mo GnRHa backbone, pointing to an ARSI effect beyond castration duration. Toxicity cost was modest (fatigue 70% vs 67%), but the screening-design α 0.10 means phase III is needed before routine 24mo enzalutamide.

open_questions: Does PFS benefit translate to metastasis-free or overall survival?
Interaction with pelvic nodal SRT and PSMA PET staging
Phase III confirmation of ARSI with SRT
